This is a great game if you like Uplink, it's very much in that mould rather than the Hacker series of games. It does have some differences. Notably, it's more linear and story-driven, in that the game seems mostly the same every time. I think IP addresses may be randomized, but other than that things like passwords seem to remain the same.

The story, so far, seems interesting. While I think ultimately I prefer Uplink's more open-ended approach towards this sort of game (the memory of my first bank heist will always be there), the one thing I can't deny is that the story of this game seems much more interesting. It also has better writing in general. 

You can find little logs and text files all over, and if you really take the time to decrypt things you'll get good payoffs for jokes. One example is a man who compared double-encrypting a file to "double bagging a condom" and if you double-decrypt one of his files, you find he tried to sue a condom company for both condoms breaking when he double bagged. A lot of the text is just bash.org quotes, but when you find the hand-crafted stuff it really delivers more than Uplink's mostly generated text.

Overall, this is an excellent game, and if you like hacking sims I seriously recommend it. Though I recommend having a pencil and paper ready for making quick notes.

While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

As an IT person, this game is redooooooooonk!
Sorry, but I can't help getting white-girl excited about Hacknet and its command-line hackerism shenanigans that are so engrossing and believable you'll start looking over your shoulder.
The game is structured around a command-line interface using Unix commands, a sort of Baby-*nix if you will.
Now, regular *nix users may criticize it simply because it's a reduction of the standard command set(switches and variables aren't implemented), but to newbies and occasional users like myself, the illusion is complete. I also appreciate the fact that it builds automatisms (like using cat for reading text) that I never really acquired - we're just missing grep and we'd have a party here,

The connections are easily made by clicking on a node in the network "map", although more hardcore players can also choose to type in "connect" followed by the IP address of the machine they wish to access.
From what I have seen so far, the writing is fascinating, the design supports the immersion experience very well, and I almost feel like I'm using my regular work tools - in a really badass way!

I feel that there's almost an educational value to this game. Suppose there was a system administration course built within this interface... wouldn't that be stupendous?

It progresses rather nicely and before you know it you are breaking into the death row records and the medical database. 
This does do a lot of things better than Uplink, but there are still some things I would have liked to see/ do in this game, like breaking into a bank. For me, it was really satisfying to break into a bank, steal all the account numbers and passwords, delete logs, steal all the money I wanted, then go buy some fancy new things. That being said, this game doesn't have any kind of money system and it seems like you are, hardware- wise, stuck with everything from the beginning ; you gather new programs by hacking into someone computers and finding them/ missions. 

One of the missions broke or something so I had a decrypt program but for whatever reason couldn't complete the mission after decrypting the indicated file. However, I then hacked the email provider, traced some emails to a computer which I broke into, stole a program, got out, and had to get back in because I ran out of time to delete the logs. 
I had to decrypt it, but I needed a password which was related to the "best character from Final Fantasy X," whose characters I had to look up because I knew none of them, and I finally decrypted/ decyphered it. The program was Clock.exe, and you know what? It was a clock. 

In short, great game if you like these kinds of games.

Great game, but too many game breaking bugs. I recommend the game because I'm looking at the intended finished product, but right now, I found several bugs that break the game or make it too easy.

If you are being traced and you finished all the hacks, and begin your PortHack.exe, you can disconnect, wait for it to finish, and it will automatically reconnect you as an admin. This can go around the servers with automatic proxy closing, or just be used to have infinite time on a server.

If you decide to investigate a little more on Naix's proxy after getting your x-server.sys back, you can scan and find his actual computer. You can find your own x-server.sys labeled as [YourName]x-server.sys under /home, and if you delete the x-server.sys under /sys then you can become friends with Naix and you will continue a short "side quest" of sorts. However, if you want to reply to the email that told you to hack Naix, it will say mission incomplete, even if you have done what it asks. No way to fix it as far as I can tell, meaning you can't advance beyond that point. This can be avoided by ignoring Naix's computer and just doing what you are told.

And on to the biggest, worst, most game breaking glitch of all. *Drumroll please*.

Once you get to the CSEC mission when Vapor wants you to look for Bit, you will find a file on his repo station that is decs encoded. If you have finished all the contracts you know how to trace the encoding to find the password for Decypher.exe, but it's unhackable. This is because it does not tell you how many ports must be open to get through, and if you open them all you will still be unable to use your PortHack.exe. This is not the glitch, settle down people. The glitch is that you are unable to reply to Vapor with the IP, meaning you can not progress from this point. There is no way to avoid it, there is no way to fix it. That's the end of the game, wait for a patch.

Please Surprise Attack, fix these glitches. Although if I may be a bit rude, you should have tested this game a bit more or released it on early access instead of making it the official release. You have some work to do, so get to it!

The gameplay itself is fun, I love it, but I just can't play more than a one hour session without being unable to progress. So this is going to be unnoticed in my Steam Library for quite some time, but I will check it occasionally to see if I can finish the rest of the game.

For those who like Uplink this is a welcome treat; A hacking game with more story, a more up to date interface that supports both mouse and keyboard controls, situations where your computer has to reboot in a more realistic manner, different interfaces to work with (just different colors and differently ordered, but still) and more.

What strikes me though, is the lack of depth the actual world has in comparison; Where Uplink had over 300 different systems connected to the internet (some of which were routers or servers with an entire local network behind them to explore), here it is a lot more limited. You also cannot upgrade your hardware, bounce your signal all over the world before hitting your target (goes to trace time), and there is no passive search (that I have noticed) going on on the background, which means that either I'm really carefull in removing my tracers or the police will never actually go looking for you.

It is however, very true to the feel of the game. So if you like your hacking games with old-school typing and none (okay, a little) of that sissy-pants clicking with mice this is definately a recommended title for your library.

Interesting side-note; You get to hack into someone's pacemaker to fullfill his wish of being euthenized. It's stuff like that that bring this game a new moral level.
